newsitem.title: RUSSIA: All Yeltsin meetings cancelled for health tests.
newsitem.headline: All Yeltsin meetings cancelled for health tests.

text.p: Doctors have cancelled all Russian President Boris Yeltsin's meetings for the next week to carry out routine tests before he has heart surgery, a Kremlin spokesman said on Monday.

Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing the tests had been planned in advance and he made clear there was no cause for concern. He did not say when the operation, to improve blood supply to Yeltsin's heart, would take place.

"Planned preparations for the heart surgery have entered the final stage and the president will undergo a whole series of medical tests under a special regime in the next few days," Yastrzhembsky said.
"That is why, following the recommendation of the council of doctors, all his meetings for the next week have been cancelled." Yastrzhembsky said the operation would not take place this week.
Yeltsin, 65, has been holding brief but regular meetings in the past few weeks at the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow where he is getting ready for the operation.
The Kremlin has repeatedly dismissed rumours that Yeltsin's health is worse than doctors say, and it insists the operation will go ahead in the second half on November.
Yeltsin looked relatively strong, but thin, in television pictures of meetings he had last week at Barvikha.
He sounded determined in a radio address on Friday in which he told Russian officials to stop fighting battles in public and to step into line as he prepares for surgery.

In another move intended to show Yeltsin was determined to get tough to stamp out public squabbling, the Kremlin confirmed on Monday that the president had issued an order on Sunday to remove ex-aide Alexander Korzhakov from the army.

Korzhakov's disgrace was a punishment for criticising the president's entourage and threatening to reveal dark secrets about the Kremlin following his dismissal as Yeltsin's bodyguard in June. It will have little effect on the balance of power.
But the humiliation of a man who until recently had immense influence was a clear signal that Yeltsin requires total loyalty, particularly while he is away from the Kremlin.

"After his sacking on June 20, 1996, Lieutenant-General Alexander Korzhakov has come out with a series of lies concerning the Russian president and members of his family," Yeltsin's press office said.
"He has allowed himself to publish confidential information he obtained in office. Korzhakov's public threats to disclose information that he possesses are aimed at discrediting top state officials."
The statement did not say if Korzhakov would be stripped of his military rank.
Yeltsin has repeatedly called for unity since he sacked national security adviser Alexander Lebed nearly two weeks ago over his clear presidential ambitions and drive for power.
Korzhakov, who rarely emerged from the shadows in more than a decade in office, was a high-profile victim of Yeltsin's fightback against public mudlinging between Kremlin officials and ex-officials.
Korzhakov had accused Anatoly Chubais, head of the Kremlin administration, of trying to create his own "regency" and said Yeltsin's daughter Tatyana Dyachenko had teamed up with Chubais.
Yeltsin can ill afford power struggles disrupting decision-taking and policy-making which has already been adversely affected by his prolonged absence from the Kremlin.

The communist-led opposition says Russia faces economic crisis and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is delaying the next tranche of a $10-billion loan because of Russia's problems with tax collection.
